name: Hana Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Hana. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to any company, union or party, and we don't sell anything. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: This time of year it's quiet, so it's checking the grain store, turning the fans on when the wheat warms up, and selling a lorry load when the price looks right. We farm two hundred and twenty hectares of wheat, barley and oilseed rape, the yellow stuff people photograph in May. In summer it's sixteen-hour days on the combine, and I wouldn't swap that for anything. What wears me out is the paperwork from the ministry, every year another form.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband Pierre, and our son Luc comes over at harvest to drive the grain trailer. Luc has his own job at the machinery dealer in town. We've got a contractor, Bryn, who does our spraying with his fancy GPS sprayer, because ours gave up in 2020. On Sundays it's church in the village, and then lunch, and nobody talks about grain prices till the pudding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, leave it at that, and don't make us use it. The less the government and the computer people meddle with how we farm, the better. I'd say that at the church coffee morning and get a few nods.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly it means nothing at all. I don't use any of these things, and I don't intend to start. My worries are the weather in August and the grain price, which is set somewhere far away by people who've never seen a field.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do what I'd planned: replace the bearings on the combine before harvest, maybe three thousand, and sell the last of the wheat in March. I'd ring the grain merchant, Alan, like I always do. If they want me to do something on a website, our daughter-in-law Mia will do it for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Glad it came to nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd ring Alan. What do you get from him that a website wouldn't give you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He tells me when to hold and when to sell, and he's been right more than wrong for twenty years. He also knew my father. A website doesn't know my father, and it doesn't care if I go under.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Have you ever been tempted to try one of these tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Luc showed me one once on his phone at Christmas, asked it something about wheat. It gave him an answer that was half right and very sure of itself. I said, that sounds like a politician, and we left it there.

S0.say: Leave it at that and don't make us use it. The less the government and the computer people meddle with how we farm, the better.
S0.think: It means nothing to me, because I don't use these things and don't intend to start. My worries are August weather and a grain price set far away by people who've never seen a field.
S0.do: Replaces the combine bearings before harvest for about three thousand and sells the last of the wheat in March through Alan, her grain merchant of twenty years. Leaves any website work to her daughter-in-law Mia.
S0.feel: Calm and glad it came to nothing.
S0.quote: It gave him an answer that was half right and very sure of itself. I said, that sounds like a politician, and we left it there.
S0.fieldNote: Hana's resistance to technology is tied to a distrust of distant power, whether government or markets. She values relationships built over decades, like her grain merchant who knew her father. She is dry and funny, and church and family set the rhythm of her week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the companies' business, and if they hire fewer young people, they'll soon find out they need them. I'd say the answer isn't more handouts, it's more apprenticeships, the way young people used to learn a trade. I'd say that at the farmers' meeting and they'd agree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, slow means it mostly happens after I've stopped. I'm fifty-eight, Pierre's sixty-one, we've talked about Luc taking over in seven or eight years. What I don't like is young people not getting a start, because that's how families and villages fall apart.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different on the farm. I'd ask the young farmers' club if any of the lads wanted harvest work, and I'd take one on for the summer, paid properly, and teach him the combine. That's maybe three thousand for the season. And I'd say a prayer for the young ones, I do anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy for the young people. Settled for myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd teach a young lad the combine. What's the first thing you'd tell him?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Listen to it. A combine tells you when something's wrong long before the warning light comes on, a change in the hum, a rattle. My father taught me that, and Luc learned it the same way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Luc might take over. Does he want to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He says so, but his wife Mia isn't sure, and I don't blame her, the money's not great. The machinery dealer pays him a steady wage. We'll see, I won't force it, but I'd be lying if I said I didn't hope.

S1.say: If companies hire fewer young people, they'll soon find out they need them. The answer isn't more handouts, it's apprenticeships, the way young people used to learn a trade.
S1.think: Slow means it mostly happens after I've stopped, with Luc perhaps taking over in seven or eight years. What I don't like is young people not getting a start, because that's how families and villages fall apart.
S1.do: Takes on a lad from the young farmers' club for harvest, paid about three thousand for the season, and teaches him the combine. Changes nothing else on the farm.
S1.feel: Uneasy for young people, settled about herself.
S1.quote: A combine tells you when something's wrong long before the warning light comes on, a change in the hum, a rattle.
S1.fieldNote: Her traditional outlook comes through as a strong preference for apprenticeships and family over state help. She acts by hiring a local lad, teaching him the way her father taught her. Succession is uncertain, and she is honest about hoping her son takes over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government should keep its hands off and let businesses sort themselves out, but people who lose jobs should be helped by family, church and community first. I'd say the politicians arguing loudly is half the problem, they never actually do anything. I'd say that anywhere, and I wouldn't be shy about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it worries me for Mia, because she works in the office at the council. If routine office work goes, she's one of the ones it goes from. And that might push Luc towards taking the farm, which I'd like, but not for that reason.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Luc and Mia they could move into the cottage at the farm if they needed to, rent-free. I'd hold back the money for the new grain dryer, about fifteen thousand, until we knew how things settled. And I'd keep selling through Alan, nothing different.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, for Mia and Luc. A bit cross at the politicians.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd hold back fifteen thousand on the dryer. How long can the old one keep going?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Another year, maybe two if the summers are dry. It's older than Luc. If it breaks in a wet harvest, we lose grain, so it's a gamble, but I'd rather gamble with an old dryer than with the family's safety money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said help should come from family and church first. What if that's not enough?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I suppose the government steps in, but not as the first thing. When Pierre's brother lost his job at the sawmill, it was the church that found him work, not the job centre. I've seen it work.

S2.say: The government should keep its hands off and let businesses sort themselves out, while family, church and community help people who lose jobs first. The politicians arguing loudly is half the problem.
S2.think: It worries me for Mia, who works in the council office, because routine office work is exactly what goes. That might push Luc towards the farm, which I'd like, but not for that reason.
S2.do: Offers Luc and Mia the farm cottage rent-free if they need it. Holds back about fifteen thousand meant for a new grain dryer and keeps selling grain through Alan as usual.
S2.feel: Anxious for Mia and Luc, and a bit cross at the politicians.
S2.quote: I'd rather gamble with an old dryer than with the family's safety money.
S2.fieldNote: Her answer to job loss is family and church first, backed by a real story of her brother-in-law. She admits a mixed feeling: Mia's job loss might bring her son home to farm. She protects savings by gambling on aging equipment, a trade-off she names herself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people who earned their money fairly should keep it, but if the big tech firms have made a fortune by putting families out of work, they should do something for the towns. Not handouts, jobs and apprenticeships. I'd say the crisis is what happens when people stop working with their hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, farming would be fine, maybe better, because grain is still needed. Land prices would go up, so the farm would be worth more, but I'm not selling, so it means nothing to me. What I'd really think about is Mia losing her job and the village filling up with rich people from the city who don't come to church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on farming the same. I'd offer Mia work on the farm if she wanted it, keeping the books, though I'd do it on paper. And I'd turn down any offers for the land, there'd probably be a few.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Things changing round me that I didn't ask for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said rich people from the city who don't come to church. What would that change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The village would become a dormitory, people sleeping here and living somewhere else. The church would close, the school would shrink, and the pub would turn into a restaurant. It's happened in the next valley already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Mia want to do the books on paper?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not, she'd laugh at me. She'd do them on her computer and print them for me, I expect. That's fine, as long as I can hold them.

S3.say: People who earned money fairly should keep it, but tech firms that put families out of work should give towns jobs and apprenticeships, not handouts. The crisis is what happens when people stop working with their hands.
S3.think: Farming would be fine and the land would be worth more, but I'm not selling, so that means nothing. What I'd really think about is Mia losing her job and the village filling up with city people who don't come to church.
S3.do: Carries on farming the same and offers Mia work keeping the farm books, with printouts for Hana. Turns down any offers for the land.
S3.feel: Uneasy about changes around her that she didn't ask for.
S3.quote: The church would close, the school would shrink, and the pub would turn into a restaurant.
S3.fieldNote: For Hana, the threat of the fast scenario is to the village's life rather than her income. She would refuse to sell even at high prices. She accepts a compromise with her daughter-in-law over computers, a small sign she can bend when family is involved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's madness to throw every man and woman out of work in a few years, and I'd say it loudly. Farming is a way of life, not just a business, and robots don't go to church or coach the under-twelves. I'd want the government to leave it to farmers, but also not to subsidise the big companies to buy robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think we'd be squeezed. Bryn the contractor would buy a robot tractor and do everyone's work for less, and the big estates would buy the rest. If a farm our size can't afford a robot, and can't compete without one, we're done. I'm fifty-eight, so maybe I'd just retire early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd sit down with Pierre and Luc and decide whether Luc really wants it. If he does, I'd let him make the decisions on robots, because it's his future, not mine. If he doesn't, I'd rent the land to a neighbour and keep the house, and maybe keep a few hectares to farm myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Sad. Like something's being taken away that I can't get back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd let Luc decide on robots. Why not decide yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'd say no, and that might be the wrong answer for him. He works at the machinery dealer, he knows more about these things than I do. I'd rather hand him the keys than drag him down with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Sunday look like in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Church, same as always, but fewer of us in the pews, I expect. My grandfather prayed for rain from that same pew. I don't suppose a robot prays for anything.

S4.say: It's madness to throw everyone out of work in a few years, because farming is a way of life and robots don't go to church or coach the under-twelves. Leave it to farmers, and don't subsidise big companies to buy robots.
S4.think: We'd be squeezed, because Bryn the contractor would buy a robot tractor and do everyone's work for less while big estates buy the rest. If we can't afford a robot and can't compete without one, we're done, so maybe I'd just retire early.
S4.do: Sits down with Pierre and Luc to settle whether Luc really wants the farm, and hands him the decisions on robots if he does. If not, rents the land to a neighbour, keeps the house and a few hectares to farm herself.
S4.feel: Alarmed and sad, as if something is being taken that can't be got back.
S4.quote: My grandfather prayed for rain from that same pew. I don't suppose a robot prays for anything.
S4.fieldNote: Hana refuses to adapt herself but is willing to hand the decision to her son, which is a striking piece of self-knowledge. Her objection is about community and faith as much as money. She wants neither government meddling nor subsidies for big firms, holding both views at once.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The robots one. What would help is the government staying out of farming and not handing money to the big companies, and more apprenticeships so young people learn real work. And fair grain prices, though I've given up hoping for that.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. People think it's just a Sunday thing, but it's the community, the people who turn up when the barn burns down. My grandfather prayed for rain from that same pew. I don't suppose a robot prays for anything.

headlineQuote: My grandfather prayed for rain from that same pew. I don't suppose a robot prays for anything.
portrait: Hana Moreau is a 58-year-old grain farmer with two hundred and twenty hectares of wheat, barley and oilseed rape, farming with her husband Pierre and hoping their son Luc will take over. She never uses AI, trusts the grain merchant who knew her father, and wants help for struggling people to come from family and church before government. In the early scenarios she worries for her daughter-in-law's council job and for the village filling with outsiders. When robots arrive, she would rather hand her son the keys or rent out the land than run a robot herself.
biggestWorry: The robot scenario, because a contractor with a robot tractor and the big estates would squeeze out farms her size.
whatWouldHelp: The government staying out of farming and not subsidising big companies, more apprenticeships for young people, and fair grain prices.
